draft.title: The Western Front
card: The Western Front was the line of trenches that ran across France and Belgium. Most Australians who fought overseas in the First World War served there, not at Gallipoli.
Both sides dug trenches and defended them with machine guns, barbed wire and artillery. Attacking across open ground, called no man's land, often led to very heavy losses.
In July 1916 Australians fought at Fromelles in France. It was their first major battle on the Western Front, and many were killed or wounded in one night.
A few weeks later they fought at Pozières, also in France. Australian casualties there were very high, and the village was taken only after heavy fighting.
draft.remember: Most Australians fought in the trenches of France and Belgium, and 1916 brought very high casualties.

a.q: Where did most Australians who fought overseas in the First World War serve?
opts: On the Western Front in France and Belgium
On the Gallipoli peninsula in Turkey
In German colonies in the Pacific
In Britain, training and guarding ports
a.why: Most Australians served on the Western Front, in France and Belgium. Gallipoli is the tempting answer because it is so well known, but the campaign lasted only eight months and involved fewer Australians.
a.clue: Think of the trench line across France and Belgium.

b.q: Why were Australian casualties so high at Fromelles and Pozières in 1916?
opts: Attacks crossed open ground under machine guns and shells
Australian troops had no trenches and no weapons at all
The battles were fought in Turkey, far from supply lines
Australian troops stayed in the trenches and did not attack
b.why: Defenders in trenches used machine guns, barbed wire and artillery, so attacks across no man's land caused heavy losses. The Turkey option is wrong because these battles were in France.
b.clue: Think about what defenders had and what attackers had to cross.

wants.why: It helps students see why attacking across no man's land was so costly.

'The village was taken only after heavy fighting' is misleading. Australians took Pozières village fairly quickly on 23 July. Most of the very high casualties came in the following weeks, from German artillery bombardment and counter-attacks while holding and pushing beyond the village.
